metadata.title: Using machine learning algorithms to predict students' general self-efficacy in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2018 microdata, merging the Student Questionnaire with the Principal Questionnaire at the student–principal level. The manuscript reports extensive data cleaning (listwise deletion for missing self-efficacy items and median imputation for missing predictors) and then trains XGBoost and Lasso using nested cross-validation, but it does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme. Because the paper does not mention weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), it is unclear whether complex survey design features were incorporated into estimation. Analysts using the PISA database should consider using the official student sampling weights and appropriate variance estimation when producing population-representative uncertainty estimates, especially given the multilevel structure (students within schools within countries).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a transformed self-efficacy score derived from five Likert items using an IRT generalized partial credit model and then linearly rescaled; the paper does not use PISA achievement plausible values (PV) for the outcome. Missing data handling is partially described: the authors explicitly apply listwise deletion for missingness on the five self-efficacy items, and they also impute missing predictor values using median substitution. Because the schema requires a single missing-data handling label, the extraction records the explicit self-efficacy-item listwise deletion as the primary strategy, while the predictor imputation is noted in the sample/preprocessing narrative.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire variables merged by linking students to their corresponding school principals. The analytic sample was restricted by listwise deletion: rows with missing data on any of the five self-efficacy items were removed (84,179 records), leaving 527,825 students. For remaining missing predictor values, the authors imputed missing predictor values by substituting median values. The final preprocessed dataset contained 256 predictors (including dummy variables) and one continuous self-efficacy outcome derived from the five items via a polytomous IRT model (generalized partial credit model) and then linearly transformed (multiply by 15; add 100).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire), self-efficacy (general) outcome
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (test set): R2 = 0.467, RMSE = 9.699, MAE = 7.219. Lasso (test set): R2 = 0.417, RMSE = 10.137, MAE = 7.683. Reduced model (top 14 predictors) R2 = 0.436; exclusion model (without top 14) R2 = 0.328.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (Student Questionnaire + Principal Questionnaire) the study leveraged mastery goal orientation, meaning of life, proud emotion, positive emotions, and learning aspiration to predict students’ self-efficacy (IRT-transformed continuous score), finding that XGBoost outperformed Lasso on the test set (R2 = 0.467 vs 0.417) and that the top predictors collectively explained a large share of variance (reduced model R2 = 0.436; exclusion model R2 = 0.328). This indicates that strengthening students’ motivational and affective supports—along with family emotional support and related socio-ecological conditions—may improve self-efficacy, though the cross-sectional design and lack of causal identification mean directionality cannot be confirmed.

data.outcome_summary: The study predicts general self-efficacy in PISA 2018 using a merged dataset of the Student Questionnaire and Principal Questionnaire. Self-efficacy is constructed from five Likert items via a polytomous IRT generalized partial credit model and then linearly rescaled, producing a continuous outcome. After listwise deletion for missing self-efficacy items (reducing the sample to 527,825 students) and median imputation for missing predictors, the authors train XGBoost and Lasso using nested cross-validation with four folds in both inner and outer loops. On the test set, XGBoost achieves R2 = 0.467 (RMSE = 9.699; MAE = 7.219), outperforming Lasso (R2 = 0.417; RMSE = 10.137; MAE = 7.683). The top 14 predictors (e.g., mastery goal orientation, meaning of life, proud/positive emotions) yield a reduced-model R2 = 0.436, while excluding them still leaves R2 = 0.328, suggesting additional indirect contributions. The paper does not report using PISA sampling/replicate weights, and the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.
